conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to make sure you feel supported and heard in these early weeks of motherhood. To do that, I’ll be using a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days so we can offer the right kind of help if you need it.  

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, except in the rare event we’re worried about immediate safety—and then we’d talk through next steps together. We’ll go through ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally and jot down your answers. There are no right or wrong responses—just whatever is true for you. Ready to begin?  

First, how have you been able to enjoy things lately—those little moments of pleasure or happiness that used to feel good before the baby arrived?

[Voice soft, a little tired]  
Honestly… not much. I’ll smile when the baby grips my finger or when my toddler does something silly, but the warm feeling fades fast. Things I used to love—like baking or putting on music and dancing around—feel kind of pointless now. I’ll try to watch a show in the evening and I just sit there thinking, “Why can’t I enjoy this anymore?”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small, tired sigh]  
I do laugh sometimes—like when my older nephew sent that goofy video—but it feels… distant? I’ll chuckle and then catch myself thinking, “Okay, that’s enough, back to worrying.” It’s not the easy, belly-laugh feeling I used to have.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quietly] Not really… I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now even those feel like chores. I’ll tell myself, “It’ll be nice,” but inside I’m just… flat. Nothing sparks that “can’t-wait” feeling anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to hands, voice small]  
Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think, “I must’ve eaten something wrong,” or “I’m not soothing him right.” Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and burst into tears because it felt like I’d failed him. I know logically it’s not a big deal, but the guilt just jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping the baby blanket tighter around my fingers]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my chest feels tight, imagining he’s stopped breathing, or I’ll picture him slipping out of my arms. There’s no real reason—it’s like my mind just spins these scary movies and I can’t hit “stop.” I try to breathe and tell myself he’s okay, but the worry keeps looping.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[speaking barely above a whisper, one hand rubbing the opposite arm]  
Yes… a few times this week it hit out of nowhere—my heart races, I feel shaky, like I need to run out of the room even though nothing’s happening. Once I was just folding laundry and suddenly pictured something awful happening to the baby; my legs went weak and I had to sit on the floor until the shaking stopped.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]  
Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish feeding him the bottles need sterilizing, the toddler wants a snack, the laundry pile is staring at me… I’ll stand in the kitchen and think, “I can’t breathe, there’s too much.” I still push through, but it’s like walking in heavy sand—every step takes everything I’ve got.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[exhales shakily]  
That’s been happening several nights. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind just… replays everything I might’ve done wrong or imagages something terrible happening to him. It takes me forever to drift off, and when I do I jerk awake with my heart pounding, sure I heard him cry—even if he’s still asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

[voice cracks]  
Yeah… a lot of the time. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be overflowing with joy, but instead I just feel empty or like I want to cry. Some mornings I wake up already sad, and it sticks around most of the day, even when nothing bad has happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes well up, voice shaky]  
Once or twice this week… like last night, I was trying to get the baby to latch and he kept pulling away, and I just started sobbing. My partner found me like that and I couldn’t even explain why—it just felt like everything was too much and I was failing him. The tears come out of nowhere sometimes, and then I feel guilty for crying when I should be “happy” he’s here.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, gaze fixed on the floor]  
Yeah… it’s popped into my head a couple times. Nothing planned—just these quick flashes, like “what if I weren’t here anymore?” or imagining driving off the road on the way to the pediatrician. They scare me. I don’t want to leave my kids, but the thoughts still sneak in when I’m feeling overwhelmed.

I hear how heavy each day feels for you right now-how even the small joys slip away quickly, replaced by worry and that constant gray cloud. You're working so hard to care for your children while battling intrusive fears, guilt, and exhaustion, and you still showed up today. That matters.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports occasional laughter but describes it as distant and quickly interrupted by worry, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring 'a lot' and gives multiple recent examples, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable anxious thoughts without external cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts multiple times this week.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed most days, unable to breathe under constant demands, and pushing through with extreme effort—matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent intrusive worries about her baby, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive sadness "most of the day" and "a lot of the time," matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm thoughts "a couple times" with vivid imagery, fitting "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 far exceeds the 14-point cutoff and is coupled with affirmative answers on the self-harm item. The narrative reveals <sym>depressed mood most of the day</sym>, <sym>loss of interest or pleasure</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness and excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> persisting nearly every day for the past week, meeting screening criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The reported <sym>panic-type episodes</sym> and <sym>intrusive catastrophic worries</sym> also suggest comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist
2. Request evaluation for <med>antidepressant medication</med> and/or therapy; both are compatible with breastfeeding
3. Develop a written safety plan with your clinician; keep crisis hotline numbers accessible
4. Share these results with a trusted support person who can stay with you until professional help begins
5. Continue gentle self-care: eat small regular meals, accept help with household tasks, aim for short outdoor walks
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress after starting treatment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screen  

Identified Symptoms / Behaviors  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, emptiness (Q8, Q9)  
- Marked anhedonia—minimal enjoyment or anticipatory pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care (Q3)  
- Intrusive anxious worries, nocturnal rumination, panic-type episodes (Q4, Q5, Q7)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “heavy,” daily functioning effortful (Q6)  
- Sleep initiation / maintenance problems linked to anxious rumination (Q7)  
- Passive self-harm ideation (transient, no plan) (Q10)  

Patterns Across Responses  
Consistent dysphoric mood with prominent anxiety, obsessive worry about infant safety, somatic tension, early-morning negative cognitions, and functional impairment in basic ADLs.  

Screening Significance  
Meets red-flag criteria for possible major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety. Passive suicidal thoughts present → elevated safety risk.  

Risk Summary  
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, psychomotor fatigue  
- Anxiety/panic symptoms multiple days/week  
- Self-harm ideation (passive)  
- Impaired bonding / parenting self-efficacy themes  

Safety Flag  
Patient endorsed fleeting thoughts of not wanting to live / hypothetical self-harm; denies intent or plan. Immediate safety assessment and follow-up indicated.
